The most prominent was Apple’s decision to expel DEICER from the App Store on the grounds that it endangered law enforcement officers; despite numerous appeals by Concepcion, Apple refused to budge. A politically motivated hacking in February made him fear for his personal safety, his financial straits grew dire enough that he had to ration his medications, and his longtime marriage ended right as his daughter was preparing to leave for college.

“I could see myself completely losing it,” he admits, describing the path he was on as “unsustainable.” But instead of retreating from the fight against ICE, Concepcion reprioritized how he could stay involved. He devoted fewer hours to coding and more to volunteering in his hometown of Syracuse, New York, where ICE raids have caused pervasive fear. He has been helping immigrants fill out power-of-attorney documents so that family members can retrieve their vehicles from impound lots if they’re ever taken by ICE. He also assists people who are attempting to contact loved ones in detention centers. When Concepcion and I spoke in October, he was trying to find a lawyer for a close friend’s brother, who’d been taken by ICE just three days earlier.

While Concepcion is coding less, he hasn’t given it up. He tweaked DEICER into a New York–specific web app called Empire Watch. He also rolled out Vote Defender, an app to disseminate citizen reports of potential problems at polling places. Concepcion is already dreaming big about the year ahead. He’s developing an app to help people study for the US citizenship test. And he’s planning to get a notary license. “I’m just trying to live my values on a person-to-person basis,” he says. —Brendan I. Koerner

Pope Leo XIV

Magnificent Humanity. Doesn’t feel that way all the time, does it? But that’s how noted Chicago White Sox fan and former math major Robert Francis Prevost titled his first encyclical as Pope: Magnifica Humanitas. Where the previous Pope Leo warned against the dehumanizing power of industrialization at the turn of the 20th century, this Leo is devoted to “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence.”

In the 42,000-word encyclical, the Pope acknowledges that “AI is already an environment in which we are immersed.” Invoking the Tower of Babel, he says humanity must reject “the pretense that a single language” can translate everything into “data and performance.” In the eyes of the Holy See, regulation alone isn’t enough. AI must be “disarmed,” Leo writes. Not by rejecting the technology but by “preventing it from dominating humanity.” And on the question of AI sentience, he’s very clear: “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences.” They don’t “feel joy or pain,” and they don’t “have a moral conscience.”

That question was reportedly a sticking point in behind-the-scenes talks between the Vatican and the AI industry. Upon presenting the encyclical in Rome, Pope Leo invited Chris Olah, an Anthropic cofounder, to speak. Olah said AI systems aren’t “engineered”—they’re “grown.” They’re “not the cold, calculating robots we were promised,” he went on. “They are made from us, from our words.”

OK, if that’s how you feel. But the AI advice Pope Leo XIV gave a Honolulu high schooler in 2025 still rings true: “Use it in such a way that if it disappeared tomorrow, you would still know how to think.” —Anthony Lydgate

Cyclosporiasis

“Diarrhea lettuce,” anyone? Of all the slang and shorthand to arrive this year, that might be the nastiest. The term started circulating in July, when a previously little-known parasite, cyclospora, began popping up in salads across the US. Officially, the outbreak—much of it traced back to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico—sickened nearly 13,000 people and hospitalized 570, but it likely afflicted many more. The news swept social media and, for a time, changed the public’s eating habits. Cyclospora’s surge also demonstrated the fragility of the US food system at a time when the country’s public health infrastructure was undergoing massive cuts. —Emily Mullin

The Bayeux Tapestry

For finally leaving France after more than 900 years—and taking out $1 billion in trip insurance.

Tom Robinson

Want to take down an online black market? Call Tom Robinson. Cofounder of crypto-tracing firm Elliptic, he’s had the operations in his sights for a couple of years. His most recent target was Xinbi Guarantee, a $24 billion Chinese-language market that sells scammers the tools they need—fake social media accounts, money-laundering services—to conduct mass-scale digital fraud. Robinson’s sleuthing helped the US Secret Service freeze cryptocurrency wallets containing more than $50 million in funds linked to Xinbi Guarantee. The marketplace has also been sanctioned and forced offline. —Matt Burgess

Madison Square Garden

For its unforgettable celebrity weddings and always-watching Eye of Sauron surveillance apparatus.

Omar Yaghi

After collecting his Nobel Prize in Stockholm late last year, Omar Yaghi returned to the United States in a restless mood. The 61-year-old chemist was thrilled to have been recognized for his pioneering work on metal-organic frameworks, crystalline structures that are built from a combination of metal ions and carbon-based molecules. And he was excited that his startup, Atoco, was testing a machine that uses these frameworks to harvest water from the atmosphere, an innovation that could completely transform the world’s driest regions. But Yaghi also feared he’d hit a dead end at UC Berkeley, where he’d been a professor since 2012. In addition to feeling constrained by the school’s bureaucracy, he was frustrated by how hard it had become to secure visas for gifted foreign students, the lifeblood of his lab. As an immigrant himself, Yaghi was troubled by the Trump administration’s virulent nativism.

“The rhetoric about immigrants is not helping good people do their job,” says Yaghi, a naturalized American citizen originally from Jordan. “I must say that for the first time in my life, I felt that I didn't have protection of the law.” So 45 years after he first came to the US as a teenager who barely spoke a word of English, Yaghi decided to find a new country in which to pursue his goal of “solving ambitious problems.”

Germany was at the top of Yaghi’s list, but none of the universities there seemed willing to provide him with the resources he wanted. He was instead lured to China: In July, Tsinghua University appointed him to lead a new institute devoted to using AI to accelerate chemical research. Yaghi says he was drawn to the opportunity because he’s a firm believer in AI’s potential to “shorten the time between discovery and commercialization.” Having spent a quarter century perfecting his water-harvesting technology, largely through arduous trial and error, he is optimistic that AI can help him get his next invention to market in a fraction of that time.

Yaghi’s move to Tsinghua was viewed as a harbinger of China’s scientific rise. And after just a few months on the school’s Beijing campus, Yaghi says he has been impressed by his colleagues’ brilliance and drive. “I feel like my scientific environment wants to get better, wants to improve, wants to move forward,” he says. “The attitude is more of a let's-get-it-done type.” Atoco is now about to start selling its first water-harvesting system, capable of producing up to 1,000 gallons per day in optimal conditions. The company is also developing machines to capture atmospheric carbon, a key to slowing the pace of climate change. These technologies use relatively little energy because Yaghi’s frameworks bond with carbon-dioxide molecules.

Yaghi still has great affection for the US, where he started his academic journey at a New York community college in the 1980s. He hopes the country will awaken to the need to protect the innovation system it built over many decades—a system he describes even now as “the envy of the world.” Science “is part of our civilization, and we should not take attacks on science very lightly,” he says. “It is something that society needs to value.” —Brendan I. Koerner

The Artemis Crew

In April, a four-person crew took a 10-day trip that circumnavigated the moon. They came back to a world with a renewed dream of space travel.

Read More

Annie Kritcher

Four years ago, Annie Kritcher achieved what, for many, would be the scientific accomplishment of a lifetime: producing net energy from a fusion reaction for the first time in history. Her wickedly cool method? Blasting a tiny target with a laser.

Her next feat may be even more awesome. She wants to use that technology to generate abundant power for all. In February, Inertia Enterprises, where Kritcher is chief scientist and cofounder, announced it had raised $450 million in Series A funding. By July, the company had opened its own facility just down the road from Lawrence Livermore National Lab, where Kritcher made fusion history and still holds an appointment.

The startup also laid out 10 milestones to track its progress and already hit two of them. Next on Inertia’s list is developing a better laser. The one Kritcher fired at Lawrence Livermore used optical fibers. Now Inertia is looking to use diodes, which are vastly more efficient. As Kritcher puts it, “If you don’t have a big laser to fire, you can’t do cool physics things.” Amen.

Inertia’s goal is to have a beam-line laser prototype—dubbed Thunderwall—ready by 2030. Kritcher refuses to pick which of their next milestones will be the most important. “They’re my little children,” she quips. She says the work has been energizing for her and her colleagues: “You want to take it all the way to the end.” Until then, Kritcher is laser focused. —Brian Kahn

Granola

For taking AI notes straight from a phone, no meeting-bot required.

Trae Stephens

For offering publicly to buy WIRED in order to improve it. Thanks, Trae, but we aren’t for sale.

IN MEMORIAM

Dolores Huerta

BORN 1930

Labor organizer, cofounder of the United Farm Workers, coiner of the phrase “¡Sí se puede!”

Gloria Steinem

BORN 1934

Feminist icon, cofounder of Ms. magazine, recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Dolly Parton

BORN 1946

Country music legend, purveyor of free children’s books, patron saint of Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

Peter Cullen

BORN 1941

Voice of Optimus Prime (and Eeyore), guided by the mantra “be strong enough to be gentle.”

Walter Koenig

BORN 1936

Chicago-born son of Lithuanian immigrants, played the USS Enterprise’s indelibly Russian officer, Pavel Chekov, in the original Star Trek.

Om Malik

BORN 1966

Accidental tech blogger turned popular commentator and venture capitalist.

Sam Neill

BORN 1947

Jurassic Park’s gruff paleontologist in a fedora, Red October’s tragically Russian first officer, New Zealand’s favorite wine grower.

Jason Collins

BORN 1978

Played 13 seasons in the NBA, including one as the first openly gay man in any of North America’s pro sports leagues.

Catherine O’Hara

BORN 1954

Emmy-winning comedic actress, pioneering weird-accent-haver, always found her Kevin.

Ted Turner

BORN 1938

Founder of CNN, American bison revivalist, Jane Fonda’s “favorite ex-husband.”

Chuck Norris

BORN 1940

Martial artist, TV lawman, MAGA hero, bipartisan punch line.

Patrick Stewart

BORN 1940

Star Trek’s engaging Jean-Luc Picard, X-Men’s Charles Xavier, creator of the best face-palm reaction meme. Legend.

Hideki Sato

BORN 1950

Nicknamed the father of Sega hardware, oversaw design of consoles like Genesis and Dreamcast.

entries.title: How a Bunch of YouTube Auteurs Are Reinventing Hollywood
entries.summary: Backrooms started as a 4chan meme. Obsession came from someone who got his start in online sketch comedy. They both got people back into theaters—and it’s just the beginning.
entries.content:
The mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.

First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.

Parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.

Though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”

Then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil.

Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he says. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.

Studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.

Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.

The YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.

What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

entries.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business
entries.summary: Google and Apple alumni Chad Steelberg and Andy Baynes are applying what they learned running software companies and designing iPhones to manufacturing lethal munitions.
entries.content:
When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion.

Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become.

Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it."

This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor.

Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate.

With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range.

Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.”

With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring, now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest, which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.”

After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

In April, Tiberius announced it had successfully fired one of its Sceptre projectiles from a NATO-standard 155-mm howitzer for the first time. It is now working with the US Army to mature the system, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license, and distribute the munition. It is also developing a missile, which it expects to start generating revenue next year.

Tiberius has turned the AI system it initially built into a product called GRAIL (Generative Real-Time Artificial Intelligence for Lethality). Steelberg says he is “most excited about” this. He hopes the platform can enable continuous upgrades to the weapon designs Tiberius licenses by decentralizing manufacturing. Steelberg says that, as well as automating supply chain management and compliance, the software simulates weapons against different targets in a range of environments and weather conditions, such as an Arctic peninsula. In addition to open-sourced data, the team is trying to get hold of much sought-after active combat data from around the world, including Ukraine. The idea is that this all enables users to test, iterate, and design weapons for specific uses much quicker.

“In the world of AI and design and development getting faster and faster, what is it that the West or the group of allied nations have an undeniable advantage on?” Baynes asks. “If you can weaponize all of the spare capacity and precision manufacturing across the UK, France, Germany, the Nordic countries, the US,” he says, “that's something that our adversaries today can never ever match.” Tiberius aims to achieve this by copying “the Apple model,” continues Baynes, who reported to Steve Jobs for four years. He says outsourcing manufacturing to many third-party subcontractors can accelerate development and deployment and keeps expensive production costs off Tiberius’ balance sheet during peacetime.

“We're taking the approach of Silicon Valley,” says Steelberg. “When you run into a big, hard, hairy problem, you not only cross that, but you turn around, you build a bridge—it’s a toll bridge, obviously—so the entire industry can cross that hurdle faster, better, stronger. They might pay a small fee, but it's better than dying in the ditch and not making it across it.”
